conventional_description: Lung cancer occurs when abnormal cells grow uncontrollably in the lung tissue, forming a tumor that can spread to other parts of the body. It is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Common symptoms include a persistent cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, and unexplained weight loss. Diagnosis is typically made through imaging tests like X-rays and CT scans, followed by a biopsy to confirm the type. Western medicine classifies lung cancer into two main types - small cell and non-small cell - and treatment is chosen based on the stage, genetic markers, and the patient’s overall health.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments include surgery to remove the tumor, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted drug therapy, and immunotherapy. The approach depends on the cancer type and stage. For advanced disease, treatment aims to control growth and manage symptoms. Palliative care is also an important part of the plan, focusing on pain relief, breathing support, and quality of life.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, lung cancer is seen as a complex interplay between a weakened body (Zheng Qi deficiency) and harmful accumulations (Xie Qi excess). The Lungs are a delicate organ, easily affected by deep sadness, overwork, or external pathogens. When lung Qi is weak, it cannot properly descend and diffuse, so fluids build up and turn into Phlegm. This Phlegm can stagnate, generate Heat, or obstruct the channels, eventually forming a mass. The Spleen and Kidneys are also deeply involved: a weak Spleen produces more Dampness and Phlegm, while weak Kidney Yang fails to warm and transform fluids.
The nature of the cough and sputum reveals the underlying pattern. White, sticky phlegm with chest heaviness suggests Damp-Phlegm clogging the Lungs. Yellow, thick phlegm with a feeling of heat points to Phlegm-Heat. A dry, hacking cough with little sputum and night sweats indicates Qi and Yin Deficiency, often seen after chemotherapy or radiation. Sharp, fixed chest pain with dark blood clots in the sputum signals Blood Stagnation. Each pattern requires a different treatment strategy - clearing Heat, transforming Phlegm, nourishing Yin, or moving Blood - rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
TCM also recognizes that lung cancer often results from a long accumulation of ‘old evils’ (latent pathogens) triggered by new factors like emotional shock, poor diet, or an infection. This ‘adding on top’ theory explains why some people develop cancer after years of chronic cough or grief. Treatment, therefore, aims not only to address the current pattern but also to resolve deeper, long-standing imbalances. By supporting the body’s own healing mechanisms, TCM helps manage symptoms, reduce treatment side effects, and improve quality of life.

tcm_diagnosis:
When a person has lung cancer, a TCM practitioner begins by listening to the cough and examining the sputum. The color, thickness, and amount of phlegm are immediate clues. A dry, weak cough with scant or no sputum points toward deficiency, while a rattling, productive cough with thick phlegm suggests an excess pattern like damp-phlegm or phlegm-heat.
Then they ask about the chest sensation. A feeling of fullness and distension that comes and goes, especially with stress, hints at Phlegm clogging the Lungs with Qi Stagnation. The pain is often dull and pressing, and the sputum may be blood-tinged. The tongue is pale and puffy with a thick white greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery and wiry.
If the dominant complaint is a heavy, tight chest with a chronic cough bringing up lots of sticky, white or clear phlegm, Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs is likely. This pattern is rooted in weak digestion, so poor appetite, bloating, and a feeling of heaviness in the body are common. The tongue is swollen with a thick white coat, and the pulse is slippery.
When phlegm turns yellow or green and feels hot, with a dry mouth and thirst, the pattern has shifted to Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs. The sputum may be blood-streaked, and the person often feels restless and feverish. The tongue is red with a yellow greasy coat, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. This often reflects an infection or tumor necrosis.
As the illness wears on, energy and fluids drain away. Qi and Yin Deficiency shows up as extreme fatigue, a feeble cough with only a little sticky sputum, and breathlessness on slight exertion. The tongue is pale or red with cracks and a thin or absent coating, and the pulse is weak and thready. Night sweats and a dry throat are also typical.
If the chest pain becomes sharp, stabbing, and fixed in one spot, Qi and Blood Stagnation has set in. The lips and nail beds may look purplish, and the tongue is dark purple with stasis spots. The pulse is choppy or wiry. This pattern indicates severe local obstruction by the tumor mass.
In advanced stages, a deep chill appears. Kidney Yang Deficiency brings an aversion to cold, cold limbs, and a pale, puffy face. The cough produces thin, watery sputum, and the person feels profoundly weak. The tongue is pale and wet, and the pulse is deep and weak. This pattern signals that the body's warming fire is failing.

patterns.pattern_name: Phlegm clogging the Lungs with Qi Stagnation
patterns.symptoms: ["Chest heaviness and fullness", "Copious white, watery sputum that is easy to cough up", "Poor appetite, bloating, and nausea", "Pale swollen tongue with thick white greasy coating", "Wheezing or gurgling sound in the throat"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or dairy-rich foods, Cold raw foods and iced drinks, Damp or humid weather, Sedentary lifestyle, Overeating
patterns.better_with: Light, warm meals, Gentle walking or stretching, Warm, dry weather or climate, Deep breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: In lung cancer, a weak Spleen fails to transform fluids, leading to the buildup of dampness and phlegm. This phlegm accumulates in the Lungs, blocking the airways and causing the local mass to grow. The obstructed Qi leads to chest stuffiness, distension, and a productive cough with copious white sputum. Over time, the stagnation can also affect blood flow, contributing to blood-tinged sputum.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale and puffy with tooth marks, thick white greasy coating. Pulse: Slippery (滑 huá), often with a wiry (弦 xián) quality at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm and dampness are heavy and sticky, produced when the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids. Greasy, cold, and damp foods further burden the Spleen, generating more phlegm, while warm, dry, and light foods assist the Spleen in transforming and transporting fluids. Movement encourages Qi to flow, preventing stagnation that allows phlegm to accumulate. A sedentary life and damp weather both contribute to stagnant Qi and external dampness invading the body. Therefore, relief comes from strengthening the Spleen, moving Qi, and keeping the body warm and dry.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and lean proteins to support the Spleen. Avoid dairy, greasy, fried, and cold raw foods that create more phlegm. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi flow and prevents stagnation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weakened by poor diet, overwork, or constitutional tendency, it fails to transform and transport fluids. These fluids accumulate into Dampness and then congeal into Phlegm, which collects in the Lungs. Over time, this phlegm obstructs the airways and can form a tangible mass, contributing to the development of lung cancer. The result is a productive cough with copious, thick, sticky white phlegm, chest heaviness, and digestive sluggishness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating, moist. Pulse: slippery (hua), like beads rolling; may feel soggy.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness is heavy and sticky by nature, and it is worsened by damp environments and foods that burden the Spleen, like dairy and grease. Warmth and movement help to transform and move dampness, while light, cooked foods support Spleen Qi, reducing phlegm production.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked, easily digestible foods. Avoid dairy, sugar, cold drinks, and greasy or fried foods, which create more dampness. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps move Qi and transform dampness. Keep the living environment dry and well-ventilated.

patterns.symptoms: ["Cough with thick yellow or green sputum", "Chest oppression and feeling of heat", "Thirst with desire to drink", "Foul-smelling sputum", "Flushed face"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or fried foods, Dairy and sugar, Smoke or pollution, Emotional stress

patterns.why_this_happens: In lung cancer, the tumor mass obstructs the airways and disrupts the normal flow of lung Qi. Fluids accumulate and congeal into phlegm. Over time, the stagnant phlegm generates heat, leading to Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs. This heat damages the delicate lung tissues, producing thick yellow or green sputum, sometimes streaked with blood, and a sensation of chest oppression and feverishness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating and red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery and rapid (滑数 huá shuò), strongest at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Heat arises when accumulated phlegm stagnates and generates heat. Cooling foods and fresh air help disperse heat, while light, non-greasy meals prevent further phlegm formation. Deep breathing exercises promote lung Qi descent and help expel phlegm. Conversely, spicy, fried, and dairy foods add heat and dampness, thickening phlegm. Smoke and pollution irritate the lungs and worsen inflammation. Emotional stress stirs up internal heat, aggravating the condition.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and dairy foods that create more phlegm and heat. Eat cooling, phlegm-resolving foods like pear, radish, and water chestnuts. Stay hydrated with warm water or light herbal teas. Gentle breathing exercises can help keep the airways open and reduce phlegm accumulation.

patterns.why_this_happens: Lung cancer and its treatments gradually exhaust the body's Qi and Yin, the vital energy and cooling fluids that keep the lungs moist and the body strong. When both are depleted, the lungs lose their ability to govern respiration properly, leading to a weak, dry cough and shortness of breath. The lack of Yin fluids causes a persistent dry mouth, while the Qi deficiency produces profound fatigue that worsens with even slight exertion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body, thin or absent coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, may be rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Yin Deficiency means the body's energy and cooling fluids are already low. Overwork and stress further consume Qi, while spicy and fried foods generate heat that burns up Yin. Rest and nourishing, moistening foods replenish both, allowing the lungs to heal and energy to return.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and gentle activities like walking or Tai Chi. Eat warm, easily digestible foods such as congee, steamed pears, and soups with astragalus root (Huang Qi) and lily bulb (Bai He). Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods that deplete Yin. Stay hydrated with warm water or herbal teas like licorice and goji berry.

patterns.worse_with: Stress and anger, Cold weather or cold foods, Sedentary lifestyle, Suppressing grief or frustration, Greasy, heavy, or processed foods
patterns.better_with: Gentle walking or stretching, Warm compress on the chest, Deep breathing exercises, Emotional expression and talking, Warm, lightly spiced meals
patterns.why_this_happens:
When Qi flow becomes stuck - often from prolonged stress, grief, or emotional constraint - it can no longer push Blood through the vessels of the chest. Over time, the stagnant Blood congeals into fixed masses, which in lung cancer manifests as the tumor itself and the severe, stabbing pain that accompanies it.
The Qi stagnation creates a distending, oppressive sensation in the chest and ribs, while the Blood stasis produces the telltale signs: purple lips and nails, a dark tongue with stasis spots, and blood-streaked sputum as fragile vessels rupture under the pressure of congealed Blood.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots (purple-blue dots or patches), distended and tortuous sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood depend on movement - physical and emotional. Gentle exercise and deep breathing physically pump Qi through the chest, loosening stagnation. Warmth dilates vessels and encourages Blood flow, while cold constricts and congeals it further. Stress, anger, and unexpressed grief are the emotional roots of Liver Qi stagnation, which directly drives this pattern, so emotional release is genuinely therapeutic. Heavy, greasy foods burden the Spleen and create more stagnation, while light, warming foods support smooth circulation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle daily movement - walking, stretching, or tai chi - is essential to keep Qi and Blood flowing. Avoid cold foods and drinks, which congeal Blood and worsen stasis. Include warming, blood-nourishing foods like dark leafy greens, beets, and small amounts of turmeric or saffron. Emotional expression matters deeply: talk through grief and frustration rather than holding them in, as suppressed emotions are a root cause of this pattern.

patterns.symptoms: ["Deep coldness in lower back and knees", "Thin, watery or clear sputum", "Frequent nighttime urination", "Aversion to cold, especially lower body", "Profound fatigue and low spirits"]
patterns.worse_with: Exposure to cold weather, Overwork and fatigue, Cold raw foods and iced drinks, Prolonged standing or sitting, Emotional stress and fear
patterns.better_with: Warmth (heating pads, warm baths), Rest and sleep, Warm, cooked meals, Gentle walking or stretching, Moxibustion on lower back
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys are the root of the body's warming Yang, and in advanced lung cancer this vital fire often fades. When Kidney Yang is depleted, the body loses its ability to transform and move fluids, so thin, watery phlegm collects in the lungs and a deep, weak cough sets in. The chest and whole body feel cold, especially the lower back and legs, because the warming function has collapsed.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the Chi (Kidney) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's warming fire, so cold environments and raw foods directly drain it, while warmth and cooked meals nourish it. Overwork and emotional stress consume Yang, but rest and gentle movement preserve it. Moxibustion on the lower back and abdomen sends heat deep into the Kidneys, rekindling the Gate of Life fire and helping the body transform fluids and generate energy again.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, cooked foods like lamb, ginger, and cinnamon. Avoid cold drinks and raw salads. Keep the lower back warm with a belt or hot water bottle. Gentle movement like walking or Qigong helps circulate Yang without depleting it.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure lung cancer?
faqs.answer: TCM is not a substitute for conventional cancer treatment, and it does not claim to cure lung cancer on its own. However, it can be a powerful complementary therapy to help manage symptoms, reduce side effects from chemotherapy and radiation, and support the body’s overall strength and resilience. Always use TCM alongside, not instead of, your oncologist’s recommended treatments.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture help with chemotherapy side effects?
faqs.answer: Yes, many patients find acupuncture helpful for managing chemotherapy-induced nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and pain. Research supports its use for these symptoms. Acupuncture is generally safe during chemotherapy, but your acupuncturist should avoid needling areas with low platelet counts or infection. Always inform both your oncologist and acupuncturist about your full treatment plan.

faqs.question: Are there any herbs I should avoid during chemotherapy or radiation?
faqs.answer: Some Chinese herbs can interact with chemotherapy drugs or affect liver enzymes that metabolize medications. For example, blood-moving herbs like San Leng or Yan Hu Suo may increase bleeding risk if your platelet count is low. It is essential to work with a qualified TCM practitioner who has experience in oncology and to share your full list of herbs with your oncologist. Never self-prescribe herbs during active cancer treatment.

faqs.question: How often should I have acupuncture for lung cancer?
faqs.answer: A typical schedule is once or twice a week during active treatment or recovery. Your practitioner will adjust the frequency based on your energy levels and symptoms. Some patients continue with monthly maintenance sessions after the initial intensive phase to support long-term well-being.

faqs.question: What is the best diet for lung cancer according to TCM?
faqs.answer: TCM generally recommends avoiding foods that create Phlegm and Dampness, such as dairy, greasy or fried foods, sugar, and cold raw foods. Instead, focus on warm, cooked meals like soups, congees, and steamed vegetables. Pears (cooked), white fungus, almonds, and lotus seeds are especially nourishing for the Lungs. If you have dryness and Yin deficiency, moistening foods like lily bulb and honey can help. Always stay hydrated with warm water.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs while on targeted therapy or immunotherapy?
faqs.answer: Some herbs may interact with targeted therapies by affecting drug metabolism. It is crucial to consult both your oncologist and a TCM practitioner who understands oncology before combining herbs with these treatments. Your practitioner can select herbs that are safe and supportive without interfering with your medication.

faqs.question: How do I know which TCM pattern I have?
faqs.answer: A TCM practitioner will diagnose your pattern through a detailed consultation, including listening to your cough, examining your sputum, checking your tongue and pulse, and asking about your energy, appetite, and emotions. The patterns described on this page are a starting point, but only a professional can accurately identify the mix of patterns that is unique to you.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for lung cancer: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials
research.description: This Cochrane review evaluated the efficacy of Chinese herbal medicine as an adjunct to conventional treatment for lung cancer. It found that some herbal preparations improved quality of life and reduced chemotherapy-related toxicity, but the overall evidence was limited by poor trial quality.
research.periodical: Chen S, Flower A, Ritchie A, et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010, Issue 3. Art. No.: CD004092.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Shenqi Fuzheng injection combined with chemotherapy for non-small cell lung cancer: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This meta-analysis of 18 RCTs involving 1,512 patients showed that adding Shenqi Fuzheng injection to platinum-based chemotherapy significantly improved overall response rate, reduced fatigue, and enhanced immune markers such as CD3+ and CD4+ T cells compared to chemotherapy alone.
research.periodical: Wang J, Li G, Yu X, et al. Journal of Ethnopharmacology. 2019; 231: 503-514.

research.title: Acupuncture for cancer-related fatigue in patients with lung cancer: a randomized, sham-controlled trial
research.description: In this trial, 120 lung cancer patients with moderate to severe fatigue received either true acupuncture or sham acupuncture for 8 weeks. The true acupuncture group reported significantly greater improvements in fatigue scores and physical function, with benefits persisting at 4-week follow-up.
research.periodical: Molassiotis A, Bardy J, Finnegan-John J, et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2012; 30(36): 4470-4476.
